stages.title: Advanced vocabulary and terminology
stages.hook: Why do doctors say "hypertension" and not just "high pressure"? Where do technical words come from?
explain: Advanced English vocabulary draws on Latin, Greek and French as well as Old English. Everyday words are often Germanic (house, water), while formal and technical words often come from Latin and Greek (domicile, hydrate). Knowing roots helps: bio (life), geo (earth), graph (write), chron (time).

Collocations and connotation matter at this level. Words like "frugal" (positive) and "stingy" (negative) have similar denotation but different connotation. Nominalisation turns verbs into nouns for formal style: "decide" becomes "decision".
stages.mnemonic: Greek and Latin roots are Lego bricks: bio + logy = study of life.
items: writing of one's own life story

gq.q: What does the Greek root "chron" mean, as in "chronology"?
Which word has a positive connotation?
gq.why: Frugal praises careful spending, whereas the others criticise.

panel.q: Why do many formal English words come from Latin and French?
o: The Norman Conquest and the later influence of Latin scholarship
English never had its own words
panel.why: After 1066 French became the language of law and power, and Latin was the language of learning.

panel.q: What is nominalisation and why is it used in academic writing?
panel.model: It turns verbs into nouns (decide to decision), giving a more formal, compact and abstract style.
panel.why: Academic style uses noun phrases.

panel.q: Which pair has similar denotation but different connotation?
panel.why: Slim is positive; skinny can sound negative.

teach.model: Many advanced English words come from Latin and Greek roots. Learn roots like bio, geo and graph to guess meanings. Notice that words with the same meaning can feel positive or negative.

points.ask: Where do these words come from?
How can I guess a word?
Do similar words feel the same?

stages.title: Academic language
stages.hook: Academic writing avoids "I think" and "a lot". What does it use instead?
explain: Academic English is formal, precise and objective. It uses hedging ("This suggests that..."), cautious verbs (indicate, appear), and avoids contractions and vague words. It cites sources to support claims.

Typical features are an impersonal style, nominal phrases, and paraphrasing. Plagiarism means presenting someone else's words or ideas as yours without credit. Summarise in your own words and give the citation. Use "however", "in addition" and "thus" to link ideas.
stages.mnemonic: Claim, cite, hedge. Say less than you can prove.
items: a note that tells the source
to say in your own words
to show something is likely, not sure
the part at the end listing sources
a short summary of a paper

o: The data suggest that sleep affects memory.
gq.why: Hedging with suggest reflects that evidence rarely proves absolutely.
Credit is the key difference between a quotation and plagiarism.

panel.q: Which is more suitable in an academic essay?
panel.why: Formal, precise word choice is expected.

panel.q: Why does academic writing hedge claims?
panel.model: Hedging keeps claims honest and accurate when evidence is limited and avoids overgeneralising.
panel.why: Epistemic caution.

panel.q: A student changes three words in a paragraph and does not cite the source. This is...
o: plagiarism, because ideas are copied without credit
panel.why: A genuine paraphrase restructures the idea in your own words and still needs citation.

teach.model: Academic writing is formal and careful. Use cautious words like suggest, give your sources, and write ideas in your own words. Do not copy without credit.

points.ask: How do I show where ideas came from?

stages.title: Professional communication
stages.hook: An email says "Please find attached the report". Why not just say "Here's the report"?
explain: Professional English values clarity, courtesy and brevity. Emails state the purpose in the first line, give details, and close with a clear next step: "I would be grateful if you could confirm by Friday." Fixed phrases such as "Please find attached" and "I look forward to hearing from you" are conventional.

Meetings use phrases like "Let's move on to the next item", "Could we circle back to this?", "I'd like to add a point". Tone is polite but direct; indirect requests (could, would) are common in British business culture, while American style is often more direct. Cultural expectations about hierarchy and small talk vary globally.
stages.mnemonic: Purpose first, politeness always, next step last.
items: to ask for a reply by a time
by the end of the day
to ask someone to check something
to be ready by a final time
a person who has an interest in a project
to say you wait for a reply
I look forward to hearing from you
sentences: I would be grateful for your reply.
Let us move on to the next item.

gq.q: Which opening line is best for a work email?
o: I am writing to confirm Tuesday's meeting.
gq.why: A clear purpose in the first sentence respects the reader's time.

gq.q: What are "minutes" in a meeting context?
o: A written record of what was discussed

panel.q: "Could you possibly send it by Friday?" compared with "Send it by Friday" is...
panel.why: Modals and softeners make requests less forceful.

panel.q: Why might a message that is polite in one culture seem too indirect or too blunt in another?
panel.model: Cultures differ in how directly they state requests and show respect, so the same words may be read differently.
panel.why: Intercultural communication.

panel.q: Which closing is most appropriate after a formal email to a client?
panel.why: Kind regards is a polite, neutral business closing.

teach.model: At work be clear and polite. Say why you are writing in the first line. Ask for what you need, and say when. End with a polite closing like Kind regards.

points.ask: How do I start an email?

stages.title: Literary analysis
stages.hook: In "Romeo and Juliet" a character says "But soft! What light through yonder window breaks?" Why does a line of 400 years ago still move readers?
explain: Literary analysis asks how language creates meaning. Look at imagery (sensory description), symbolism, tone, narrative voice, structure and theme. Shakespeare used iambic pentameter: ten syllables in five unstressed-stressed pairs. This line gives a natural rhythm to speech.

A close reading quotes short pieces of text and explains their effect: "The word 'yonder' evokes distance, adding longing." Distinguish the author from the narrator. Consider context - when and why a text was written - but support interpretations with evidence from the text.
stages.mnemonic: Quote it, name the technique, explain the effect.
items: language that appeals to the senses
the voice that tells the story
a long speech by one character alone
an object that stands for an idea
a repeated pattern of sound at the start of words
a main idea in a text
contrasting what is said and what is meant
five pairs of syllables in a line

gq.q: How many syllables are in a line of iambic pentameter?
gq.why: Penta means five; each iamb has two syllables, so ten.

gq.q: A character says "What lovely weather" during a storm. This is...
gq.why: The words mean the opposite of what is clear.

panel.q: Which is an interpretation supported by evidence?
o: The repeated image of darkness suggests fear, as in lines 3 and 9.
panel.why: A strong reading ties a claim to specific textual details.

panel.q: Why is the narrator not always the same as the author?
panel.model: The narrator is a voice created by the author and may have views, limits or biases that the author does not share.
panel.why: Narratological distinction.

panel.q: Why does a literary critic consider the historical context of a text?
o: It can help explain the ideas and the language
panel.why: Context informs but does not replace close reading.

teach.topic: How to analyse a literary text
teach.model: Read closely and notice the techniques the writer uses, like imagery or symbol. Quote short pieces of text. Explain what effect each one has on the reader. Keep the author and narrator apart.

points.ask: How do I support my point?

stages.title: Advanced listening comprehension
stages.hook: Why do fast speakers seem to swallow whole syllables? Does the speech still carry meaning?
explain: Advanced listening means understanding authentic speech: reductions ("gonna", "wanna"), assimilation (ten bikes becoming "tem bikes"), elision ("next day" without the t) and varied accents. You rely on context, stress and intonation to fill gaps.

Strategies: predict from the topic, note key words, tell fact from attitude. In lectures, listen for signposts ("The second point is...") and for stress on new information. Understanding accents from Scotland, Nigeria, India or the USA improves with exposure.
stages.mnemonic: Ears hear sounds; the brain adds meaning.
items: a joining of sounds across words
losing a sound in fast speech
a sound changing because of the next sound
speech that is natural, not scripted
sentences: I am not gonna be late.
Her accent is easy to follow.

o: Dropping a sound in connected speech
gq.why: In "next day" the /t/ is often dropped.

gq.q: How does a lecturer usually signal the main points?
o: With signposts such as "The second point is"

panel.q: Why can "wanna" appear in speech but is avoided in formal writing?
o: It is a casual spoken reduction of want to
panel.why: Reduced forms belong to informal register.

panel.q: How can you cope when you miss a word in a recording?
panel.model: Use context and key words to guess the meaning and keep listening rather than stopping.
panel.why: Bottom-up and top-down processing.

panel.q: Which speaker attitude is shown by rising pitch and the word "Really?" in disbelief?
panel.why: Intonation conveys attitude beyond the words.

teach.model: Real speech is fast and sounds join together. Use the topic and key words to guess meaning. Listen for stress and the speaker's attitude. Get used to different accents by listening often.

stages.title: Oral fluency and presentations
stages.hook: How can you speak for two minutes about a topic without a script?
explain: Fluency is not speed; it is a smooth flow with few long pauses. Fillers such as "well", "you know" and "let me think" buy time. Organise with a simple frame: introduce, give two or three points with examples, conclude.

In presentations, vary pitch and pace, use pauses before key points, and stress important words. Practise chunks (fixed phrases) like "As far as I'm concerned" or "The main reason is that" to speak more naturally. Record yourself and review.
stages.mnemonic: Chunks, not words: speak in ready-made phrases.
items: a phrase that keeps flow while you think
as far as I am concerned
Today I would like to talk about
I would be happy to take questions
sentences: Today I would like to talk about health.
As far as I am concerned, it matters.

o: A ready-made group of words used together
gq.why: Using chunks makes speech faster and more natural.

o: A pause before a key point
gq.why: A pause gives emphasis and lets the audience think.

panel.q: Which is true about fluency?
o: It means smooth flow, not just speed
panel.why: Fluent speakers can pause and still be fluent; it is about flow and ease.

panel.q: How can recording yourself help your speaking?
panel.model: You can hear your pace, pronunciation and filler words and then improve them.
panel.why: Self-monitoring.

panel.q: Which is a good conclusion for a talk?
o: To sum up, there are three main reasons to act now.
Well, that is all, I think.
panel.why: A concise summary reinforces the main message.

teach.model: To speak smoothly use ready-made phrases. Have a plan: introduction, main points, conclusion. Pause before important ideas and look at your audience.

stages.title: Translation and interpretation
stages.hook: A Spanish speaker says "Tengo hambre" - literally "I have hunger". How should you translate it?
explain: Translation transfers meaning across languages; interpretation does it orally. Translators study text type, audience and purpose. They choose strategies: borrowing, calque, equivalence, adaptation. "Tengo hambre" becomes "I am hungry," not "I have hunger," because English uses be.

Interpreters work consecutively (speaker pauses) or simultaneously (almost real time). Skills include memory, note-taking and quick decisions. Ethics: accuracy, impartiality and confidentiality. When meaning is unclear, a translator may add a note or ask the client.
stages.mnemonic: Meaning in, meaning out. Faithful but natural.
items: to put written text into another language
to put spoken words into another language
a word-for-word copy of a foreign phrase
sentences: Translate the meaning, not the words.

gq.why: Source is the original; target is the result.

gq.q: Which is the best English translation of Spanish "Tengo hambre"?

panel.q: Why is a pun hard to translate?
o: It depends on sound or double meaning in one language
panel.why: The wordplay rarely works in another language.

panel.q: Why must interpreters be impartial and keep information confidential?
panel.model: Parties must trust that the interpreter conveys messages accurately and keeps private information safe.
panel.why: Professional ethics.

panel.q: Which interpreting mode is used at a long speech at the United Nations?
panel.why: Interpreters work almost in real time via headsets, so the meeting continues.

teach.model: Translating changes written text from one language into another, and interpreting does it for speech. The aim is to keep the meaning. Interpreters stay neutral and keep things private.

stages.title: Idiomatic and figurative language
stages.hook: "The pen is mightier than the sword." Is the pen really a weapon? What does figurative language add?
explain: Figurative language goes beyond literal meaning: metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole, understatement, metonymy ("the crown" for monarchy) and idiom. A dead metaphor like "the leg of a table" is so common we no longer notice it.

Idioms from many sources enrich English: sports ("on the ball"), sailing ("learn the ropes"), and Shakespeare ("a foregone conclusion"). Meaning can shift: "literally" is now often used for emphasis, which some speakers criticise. Language change is normal.
stages.mnemonic: Literal says it; figurative shows it.
items: using a related thing to mean another
a metaphor so common we no longer notice
to relax tension in a meeting
sentences: I have told you a million times.
The wind whispered through the trees.

gq.q: "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse" is an example of...
"The White House announced a decision" uses...
gq.why: The building stands for the government.

panel.q: "It's a bit chilly" said in a blizzard is...
panel.why: Saying less than the truth creates irony or humour.

panel.q: Why are idioms often confusing for non-native readers?
panel.model: Their meaning is not the sum of the words and depends on cultural convention, so literal reading misleads.
panel.why: Figurative language relies on shared knowledge.

panel.q: Why is "the leg of a table" called a dead metaphor?
o: People no longer notice it is a metaphor
panel.why: Its figurative origin is forgotten.

teach.model: Figurative language means something other than the literal words. A metaphor says one thing is another. Hyperbole exaggerates. An idiom is a fixed phrase with a special meaning.

stages.title: Extended independent writing
stages.hook: How do you turn a blank page into 800 words of independent writing?
explain: Independent writing follows a process: plan, draft, revise, edit. Plan by brainstorming and outlining. Draft without worrying about errors. Revise for content and organisation, then edit for grammar, spelling and punctuation.

Strong writers vary sentence length, use precise verbs, and show rather than tell: "Her hands shook" rather than "She was nervous." Choose a clear purpose (inform, argue, narrate, describe) and write for a specific reader. Cohesion (linking) and coherence (logical flow) make a text read well.
items: to show with detail not statement
sentences: Her hands shook as she spoke.

gq.why: Revision of content follows the draft; editing comes later.

o: Her hands shook and her voice cracked.
gq.why: Concrete details let the reader infer the emotion.

panel.q: What is the difference between revising and editing?
o: Revising improves ideas and organisation; editing fixes surface errors
panel.why: Revise first for big issues, then edit for details.

panel.q: Why should you write for a specific reader?
panel.model: It helps you choose the tone, level of detail and vocabulary that suit the reader and purpose.
panel.why: Audience awareness.

panel.q: Which is an example of poor cohesion?
o: Ideas that jump between topics with no linking words
A logical order with linking words
panel.why: Cohesion depends on links between sentences.

teach.model: Write in steps: plan, draft, revise and edit. First get ideas on paper. Then improve the ideas and order. Last, correct grammar and spelling. Think about your reader.
